content: New genotypes of lyssaviruses have been identified, and quantitative criteria for their differentiation have been proposed. To address the increasing diversity of rabies-related viruses, the genus Lyssavirus was established under the guidance of the International Committee on the Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV). The name Lyssavirus originates from Greek mythology, where Lyssa (Λύσσα) was a goddess or spirit associated with rage, fury, and madness. The genotypes initially served as a foundation for the taxonomy of lyssaviruses but were later refined to align with the ICTV's official rules, which apply to more complex entities like viral species. Recently, the nomenclature of the genus was updated to define each species as a distinct Lyssavirus. The criteria for distinguishing lyssavirus species include genetic distance, with thresholds of 80–82% nucleotide identity for the complete N gene or 80–81% for concatenated coding regions of the N, P, M, G, and L genes. Isolates within the same species generally exhibit higher identity values than these thresholds, except for viruses within the Lagos bat lyssavirus species. Some researchers have suggested subdividing this species into multiple genotypes, but due to insufficient demarcation characteristics, Lagos bat lyssavirus remains a single species, as its representatives form a monophyletic cluster in most phylogenetic analyses. Additional criteria include the topology and consistency of phylogenetic trees derived from various evolutionary models, antigenic patterns based on reactions with nucleocapsid monoclonal antibodies (preceded by serological cross-reactivity and serotype definition using polyclonal antisera), and, when available, ecological properties, host range, geographical distribution, and pathological features. Currently, the ICTV recognizes 14 species within the Lyssavirus genus, which are divided into three phylogroups based on genetic distances and serological cross-reactivity. Phylogroup I includes rabies lyssavirus (RABV), European bat lyssaviruses 1 and 2, Bokeloh bat lyssavirus, Duvenhage lyssavirus, Australian bat lyssavirus, Aravan lyssavirus, Khujand lyssavirus, and Irkut lyssavirus. Phylogroup II contains Lagos bat virus, Mokola virus, and Shimoni bat virus, while phylogroup III includes West Caucasian bat lyssavirus and Ikoma lyssavirus. Two additional viruses, Gannoruwa bat lyssavirus (isolated from Pteropus medius bats in Sri Lanka) and Lleida bat lyssavirus (from a common bent-winged bat in Spain), are likely to be classified within the genus. Gannoruwa bat lyssavirus is closely related to RABV and Australian bat lyssavirus, while Lleida bat lyssavirus is highly divergent and clusters with phylogroup III viruses, such as Ikoma lyssavirus and West Caucasian bat virus. Two cases of Taiwan bat lyssavirus have been reported in Japanese house bats (Pipistrellus abramus) in Taiwan, but further genetic data are needed before it can be proposed as a separate lyssavirus species. Similarly, Kotolathi bat lyssavirus, isolated in Finland, requires further characterization before formal classification. The ongoing discovery of lyssaviruses in bats supports the hypothesis that all lyssaviruses originated in bats. While bats are the reservoir hosts for 15 of the 17 recognized and proposed lyssavirus species, neither Mokola nor Ikoma lyssavirus has been detected in bats, and their reservoir hosts remain unknown. Lyssaviruses exhibit broad antigenic cross-reactivity at the nucleocapsid level due to the conserved sequence of the N protein, allowing similar reagents to be used for immunofluorescence-based diagnosis. However, the ectodomain of the G protein, which contains the main antigenic sites, is more variable. Cross-neutralization occurs among lyssaviruses within the same phylogroup (amino acid identity in the ectodomain >74%) but not between phylogroups (identity <62%). Experimental evidence indicates that current vaccine strains, all of which belong to the RABV species in phylogroup I, are ineffective against infections caused by lyssaviruses in phylogroups II and III.
